endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Vendors should be contractually obligated to disclose known limitations, risks, and performance characteristics of their AI solutions or systems — including subgroup performance variability, out-of-distribution behavior, conditions under which the model should not be used, and any known safety concerns identified during validation.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: iii) Clear descr iption of problem formulation and intended use accompanied by clear and detailed instructions for use.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence and Enhanced Recovery After Surgery as Patient Safety Strategies for Perioperative Care in Resource-Limited Settings
endorsements.quote: Procurement decisions should require evidence of clinical scope, data requirements, human oversight, cybersecurity safeguards, bias assessment, local validation plans, and post deployment monitoring.

endorsements.title: Feasibility-First Risk Management for Clinical AI: A Deterministic Systems Intelligence Framework for Release, Monitoring, Rollback and Withholding
endorsements.quote: Purchasers should require vendors and implementing organisations to provide an admissibility dossier before routine deployment: intended-use boundaries, model and data provenance, local data-fit checks, subgroup and equity-risk review, workflow-load assessment, monitoring metrics, incident-reporting channels, version-control procedures and pre-specified rollback thresholds.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources, one framework, one guidance document, and two commentaries, endorse requiring vendors to disclose intended use, problem formulation, intended population and setting, and conditions of non-use, but no supplied study tests whether this requirement changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes. No supplied study documents how often purchasers deploy tools in contraindicated conditions because vendor information was missing.

perspectives.view: The supplied record contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The endorsements come from a framework, a guidance document, and two commentaries, which are expert opinion under GRADE conventions. Their agreement shows consensus on the idea but cannot establish an effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The recommendation assumes that missing vendor information leads to use in contraindicated conditions, and that disclosure prevents it. Neither step has supplied data behind it. A disclosure document may catch errors only if someone reads it and checks it against local conditions before go-live, and the supplied sources do not report whether that happens.

The supplied endorsements rely on contractual obligation and procurement requirements rather than statute or regulation. The CHAI playbook frames disclosure as a contract term, and one commentary proposes an admissibility dossier before routine deployment. No supplied source reports how such contract terms are enforced or whether vendors comply.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments made with and without structured vendor disclosure of intended use and contraindicated conditions, and none measures the frequency of off-label or out-of-scope AI deployment. A useful first study would audit current contracts and deployed tools to estimate how often use falls outside vendor-stated scope, followed by a comparison of sites that require disclosure against sites that do not.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. One endorsing commentary addresses resource-limited perioperative settings, but it offers opinion rather than data, and whether disclosed intended populations actually include these groups remains unexamined.
